channel.title: Nature Human Behaviour
channel.description: Drawing from a broad spectrum of social and natural science disciplines, Nature Human Behaviour will publish research of outstanding significance into any aspect of human behaviour, its psychological, biological, and social bases. How do humans perceive, think, feel, decide, and act? How do they interact with their environments and others? How do these abilities develop and decline over the lifespan? How do they evolve and compare with other species? How do they vary among individuals, groups, and cultures? How are they shaped by socioeconomic and political factors? How are they affected by disease or deprivation? What interventions can influence individual behaviours or outcomes? The journal welcomes research from any discipline that provides significant original insight into these questions.

item.title: The future of large-scale experiments and their challenges in the digital era
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02582-6

Large-scale experiments now underpin much of modern social science. This Perspective highlights six emerging challenges and suggests directions for future research.

item.title: A research agenda for making evidence useful, usable and used in policymaking
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02593-3

Bridging the gap between evidence production and policy impact requires understanding how evidence becomes useful, usable and used. Spohn et al. discuss the obstacles and set a research agenda for evidence adoption.

item.title: Loneliness and desire for thinness explain sex differences in adolescent internalizing problems
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02578-2

Girls tend to show higher rates of depression and suicidal ideation than boys. This work suggests that loneliness and pressure to be thin explain much of this gap, suggesting that social factors are key targets for youth-focused support, policy and intervention.
item.dc:title: Loneliness and desire for thinness explain sex differences in adolescent internalizing problems

item.title: Building health-literate artificial intelligence
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02595-1

Can AI do more than deliver health information? This Perspective argues that AI should be designed to support understanding, informed decision-making and action, placing health literacy at the centre of AI design and governance.

item.title: Large estimated size of the Australian Indigenous population before its extensive decline following colonial invasion
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02571-9

Before the British invasion in 1788, Australia’s Indigenous population is estimated to have numbered about 2.2 million people, exceeding previous estimates. An estimated 2.06 million excess deaths occurred between 1788 and 1861.
item.dc:title: Large estimated size of the Australian Indigenous population before its extensive decline following colonial invasion
